parsed.stack: Ray-Ban Display third-party HTML/CSS/JS app with Neural Band input, paired with an iOS/Android companion (React Native) that does the work: on-device vision to recognise the part, on-device ASR for the spoken note, all at zero marginal cost. Local SQLite plus optional iCloud/Drive backup - the teardown history never leaves the user's devices. One-time purchase $29.99 (price_month below is that amortised over 12 months).
milestones: Week 1-3: Display app shell, Neural Band gestures for 'pin this' and 'show me what was here', glanceable card layout.
Week 4-6: capture pipeline - photo plus spoken note pinned to a named part, with the part hierarchy (assembly > sub-assembly > fastener).
Week 7-9: re-surfacing during reassembly: look at the frame, get back the notes taken while removing from that area, in reverse order.
Week 10-11: export a shareable teardown log (the artefact that does the marketing) as a web page.
Week 12: 10 restorers who already own the hardware, one full teardown each.
parsed.riskiest_technical_assumption: That the Display's camera and on-device vision can re-identify a specific spot on a stripped frame months later, without fiducial markers - visual anchoring on an object that is being progressively disassembled is the hard version of the problem, because the scene deliberately changes.
parsed.cheapest_way_to_test_that_assumption: Borrow or buy one Display, photograph 20 locations on a bike at teardown and again at reassembly six weeks later, and measure how often the on-device matcher returns the right pinned note - no app needed, just a script over the photo pairs.
